topicA.name: AI Search Visibility and Brand Discovery

resources.headline: AI Knows Your Brand – It Rarely Puts You On The Shortlist via @sejournal, @gregjarboe
resources.fullText: Tony Uphoff ran a test this month that every SEO and brand manager should copy before next year’s planning starts. He asked ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews the questions his prospective clients ask, then counted how often the answer engines recommended the two businesses he launched in February. The results were humbling. Across 59 answers, his newsletter, Uphoff on Media, showed up in zero of 12 category answers. His firm, Uphoff Advisory, showed up in one of 43. Yet every engine that answered “Who is Tony Uphoff?” knew his career. Tony said “The models know who I am. They almost never recommend what I’ve built.” That gap, between being known and being recommended, is the measurement problem I think most of our industry is still getting wrong. Tony’s test shows you how to find it in your own brand, and three other posts he published in October explain why your CFO, your next acquirer, and your next employer are about to care about it. From A Certain Point Of View, We’re On The Same Beat A disclosure first. Tony and I worked together at Ziff-Davis from 1988 to 1993, and he’s since been CEO of five businesses. He was brought in to transform Business.com and ThomasNet.com, led the carve-out of Pipeline360, where he now serves as a board advisor, and today writes Uphoff on Media while running Uphoff Advisory. His audience is B2B media, marketing, and technology operators, not SEO specialists. But read his last four posts back to back, and you’ll find a five-time CEO working through the same questions this column keeps asking about AI search, from the other side of the table. Bill Ziff taught a generation of us at Ziff-Davis to separate events from trends. Tony’s October 7 headline, “AI Stopped Being a Story. Now It’s in Your Multiple,” is that lesson in 10 words. When AI shows up in the valuation of a company, it has stopped being an event. See also: The Click Economy Is Over: How AI Search Is Forcing Publishers To Rethink Revenue Search Changed Jobs, And The Scoreboard Didn’t Tony’s argument starts with a sequence change in B2B buying. “The machine drafts the shortlist. The human validates it.” The survey data backs him up. In G2’s March 2026 survey of 1,076 B2B software buyers, 51% said they now start their research with an AI chatbot more often than with Google, up from 29% in G2’s 2025 report. 69% said a chatbot led them to choose a different vendor than they had planned, and one in three bought from a vendor they had never heard of before. Here is where Tony makes the point I’d underline for every SEO reading this. “For two decades the scoreboard was discoverability. SEO taught every marketing team to rank, earn the click and get found. Most companies carried that scoreboard straight into AI.” They ask a model about themselves by name, get an accurate answer, and conclude they’re covered. Tony calls that a false positive, and his own results prove it. A well-known founder or a legacy brand makes the business feel visible. Ask what a buyer would actually ask, and the company rarely makes the list. In my columns on YouGov’s AI brand research, I’ve kept coming back to one idea. Awareness is not the metric that tells you who is winning. Consideration is. Tony’s discoverable-versus-recommended split is the same funnel distinction, measured inside the answer engine. If brand recognition is doing that little of the work, then a report built on branded queries is measuring the wrong thing. See also: Brand Protection In AI Search: How To Audit And Defend Your Brand’s Identity Answer Engines Describe The Company You Used To Be The second finding should worry anyone who has been through a rebrand, a merger, or a leadership change. Tony called out that “all three engines that described me still call me CEO of Pipeline360.” Only one mentioned the firm he runs now. He explained, “The sources included org-chart aggregators, executive databases and old press releases.” Tony’s rule of thumb is blunt. Answer engines default to what the web has said about you most often, “and most often usually means longest ago.” That stale record costs twice, because the machine uses it to decide whether to recommend you and the human uses it to verify the machine. Few teams are watching. A Corporate Ink study reported by eMarketer in May found only 29% of marketers actively track and measure AI visibility. There’s a second lesson buried in Tony’s test. When he asked the engines “What is Demand-as-a-Service?” all three defined it accurately and cited Pipeline360’s own pages. None mentioned Tony, who helped create the strategy. He’s fine with that, because the company owns the category language. But his conclusion is the one content strategists should tape to the monitor. “The models credit whoever publishes the clearest explanation, not whoever had the idea first.” See also: AI Visibility Measurement: What To Track & What To Ignore AI Shortlists Are Built From Other People’s Shortlists The one time Uphoff Advisory made a list, ChatGPT ranked it second of four for “Who advises founders of B2B information and data businesses?” The broad questions returned nothing. The citations explain why. On category questions, the models rarely cited the firms they named. They cited roundups, the “best AI newsletters” and “best B2B marketing podcasts” lists published by Zapier, Content Allies, and others. Tony points to a May 2026 study by Maryanna Franco and João da Silva on Friction AI’s platform that found the same mechanism at scale across 14,140 queries about activewear brands. Nike and New Balance share the same Google Knowledge Graph description, yet Nike appeared in about 71% of athleisure recommendation answers and New Balance almost never did. This is where I’d push back on Tony a little. Nineteen prompts run for one week is a snapshot, and AI answers shift from run to run. One appearance in 43 could be a floor or it could be noise, and a single week can’t tell you which. His plan to rerun the same promp
keyNotes: Even if AI knows who you are, it might not recommend your business; one person found his newsletter was never recommended in 12 categories, and his advisory firm only once out of 43 times, despite AI knowing his career.
More than half of business buyers (51%) now start their research with AI chatbots, and most of them (69%) end up choosing a different company than they originally planned because of the chatbot.

Businesses used to focus on just being 'discoverable' online, meaning getting found easily, but now it's more important for AI to actually suggest your company when someone asks for solutions, not just know about you.

AI often uses old information, like past job titles or old press releases, to decide what to recommend, meaning what the AI says about you might not be current, and only 29% of marketers are actively checking this.

AI tends to recommend companies that provide the clearest explanations of a topic, rather than the company that first came up with the idea, and it often gets its recommendations from existing 'best of' lists published by other websites.
resources.question: Considering Tony Uphoff's finding that AI knows who he is but rarely recommends his current businesses, how might your own company ensure AI recommends your most relevant and current offerings, rather than just knowing your past?

resources.headline: Big Brands Dominate AI Search But Leave Openings For Smaller Sites via @sejournal, @martinibuster
resources.fullText: New research from BrightEdge shows that top brands in travel categories dominate the rankings in both ChatGPT and AI Overviews. What’s interesting is that while the BrightEdge data shows that the same brands are dominating travel queries, the top-ranked brands differ according to which sector/niche of travel is being inquired about. Big Brands Lead Their Sectors What people choose has generally been biased toward whatever is the most well known. That’s the idea behind advertising, that the more well known a product is, the likelier it is to be chosen by a consumer, and if the consumer is delighted by the choice, they’ll generally stick with that choice (brand loyalty). So it shouldn’t be surprising that big brands that are well known and trusted by consumers win out for each of their given sectors. BrightEdge data shows: “American Airlines, Royal Caribbean and Expedia lead their categories on both Google AI Overviews and ChatGPT. Hotels have a different leader on each engine. Hilton leads Google AI Overviews at 28.3%. Marriott leads ChatGPT at 29.4%. 2.2x: Expedia’s visibility compared with Kayak on Google AI Overviews (31.3% vs 14.4%). On ChatGPT, the gap is 1.4x. 38%: share of booking-intent prompts on Google AI Overviews that name a booking platform, against 12% of inspiration prompts. 78%: Booking platforms appear in 78% of budget-related Google AI Overviews answers, compared with 17% of other answers. 9%: Only 9% of tracked Google AI Overviews prompts have booking intent.” Then elsewhere it shows how brands dominate their categories: Airlines. American Airlines leads on Google AI Overviews (26.6%) and ChatGPT (25.3%). Its gap to United is 6.1 points on Google AI Overviews and 9.1 points on ChatGPT. Cruise lines. Royal Caribbean leads on both engines, at 24.8% and 28.8%. Royal Caribbean and Carnival have higher visibility in this ChatGPT sample, while Viking has lower visibility.” Lastly, the BrightEdge data shows where smaller brands may have an uphill fight competing: Queries with the word “cheap.” “Booking platforms appear in 78% of tracked Google AI Overviews answers involving terms such as “cheap,” “deal,” “budget” or “last-minute,” compared with 17% of other answers. Expedia appears in 44% of the budget-related answers. The pattern suggests that price-focused questions are an important area for booking platforms to track. It is an observed association, not evidence that using these words causes a brand to appear.” One additional thing to point out is that AI search doesn’t link out to sites with rankings in the same way that classic Search does. This is why BrightEdge calls these figures share of voice, rather than rankings of individual search results. They measure appearances among tracked AI answers because AI does not feature traditional ranking positions. Inspiration Questions: Human Subjectivity Adding further complexity to understanding the AI results is that the results containing user generated content (UGC) and content with a human experience quality to it tend to rank better for queries that are related to inspiration. There is less domination of big brand rankings for subjective queries, which creates and opening for sites like Reddit and YouTube. While BrightEdge did not speculate as to the reason why big brands don’t show for those kinds of queries, it may be that queries that require human experience are not the kinds of queries that big brands focus on. That data point may be a bright spot not just for forums and Reddit but also for travel blogs and smaller travel-related sites that can be subjective and can add unique human insights and subjectivity. BrightEdge says this about what their data shows: “Platforms and organizations such as YouTube, Reddit and AAA are more prominent in inspiration questions. Hotels and cruise lines feature more heavily in comparison questions, while booking platforms appear more often in booking-intent questions. Only 9% of tracked Google AI Overviews prompts fall into the booking-intent category. Inspiration and comparison account for most of this panel, making them important areas for travel brands to measure visibility and competition.” That means there is an opening for smaller and rising brands to cover areas where human experience, human judgement, and subjective opinion based on experience is valued and sought after by consumers. Queries that clearly belong in specific categories tend to be dominated by big brands. Like regular search though, the key to breaking into most any niche is to grow awareness of a brand and build trust. Search engine rankings are heavily influenced by user behavior signals and those rankings are then fed up the pipeline to AI chat. BrightEdge observes: “Categories: hotels, airlines, booking platforms and cruise lines. Non-travel platforms such as YouTube and Reddit are excluded from the category rankings.” The door into ranking is inspiration and subjectivity, the kinds of things that Reddit tends to rank for. That said, UGC and platform rankings have historically been vulnerable to smart and aggressive content strategies, so I would encourage travel bloggers to eat Reddit’s lunch with expertise because expertise and authoritativeness has never been Reddit’s strength. Read the full findings at BrightEdge: Holiday Travel in AI Search: The Travel Brands AI Puts on Its List Featured Image by Shutterstock/RogerYebuah Category News SEO AI Search
keyNotes: Big, well-known companies like American Airlines and Expedia often appear first in new AI search tools (like ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews) for travel questions, much like how famous brands usually get chosen in regular shopping.

However, there's a big opportunity for smaller websites and blogs in AI search when people are looking for "inspiration" – things like personal experiences or opinions – because big brands don't dominate these kinds of searches as much.

For example, only 9% of the travel searches tracked on Google AI Overviews were about actually booking something; most people were looking for ideas or comparisons, which is where unique human stories can really stand out.
If you're a smaller business, it's very hard to compete with huge booking platforms when people search for "cheap" deals, as these big companies show up in 78% of those budget-related AI answers.
resources.question: The article suggests that smaller sites can succeed in AI search by providing "human experience, human judgement, and subjective opinion." In your own field, where do you think genuine human insight or personal stories are most valued by your audience, and how could you share those in a way that stands out?

resources.headline: AI Search Is Growing Faster Than Its Business Model
resources.fullText: < Featured Blogs Home > Featured Blogs > AI Search Is Growing Faster Than Its Business Model AI Search Is Growing Faster Than Its Business Model Big Tech earnings this week put a spotlight on the monetization dilemma at the heart of AI-integrated search. The growth of Google’s AI Mode is proving to be a double-edged sword: Investments in conversational search are fueling Google’s fastest year-over-year search query growth in five years, but the company’s advertising revenue growth slowed to 12%, its slowest rate in five quarters. Google hasn’t lost its advertising engine. Search revenue is still growing. But AI is beginning to decouple query growth from monetization growth while simultaneously reducing the referral traffic that has historically supported monetization across the open web. For example, Reddit CEO Steve Huffman said Google search referrals declined “meaningfully” in Q3 because of consumers staying within AI Mode and AI Overviews, rather than clicking through to publishers’ sites. Reports from Reddit’s earnings call put the October decline at more than 1 million referrals per week on average. More Ads Could Put AI Search’s Trust At Risk For Google, AI Mode currently has far fewer ads than classic search, so an obvious solution is to add ads to AI-integrated results pages. The company announced plans to scale ads in both AI Mode and AI Overviews across a wide range of queries, expand ads into international markets for the first time, and launch multi-turn ads in AI Mode, where sponsored results appear in follow-up questions, across the US. While Google says click-through rates are similar between sponsored and organic search results in AI Mode, just adding more ads to AI-integrated search risks the trust consumers have in answers, which is what drives query growth. According to Forrester’s data, 70% of US and UK consumers who regularly use answer engines trust the answer provided by the answer engine. That could erode if consumers begin to question whether advertising and sponsored results influence the answers AI generates. The Monetization Gap Will Accelerate Conversational Advertising This tension reinforces one of Forrester’s latest media predictions: Conversational ads will become a multibillion-dollar channel. We expected answer engines to turn aggressively toward advertising as user growth moderates and engine providers shift their focus from acquiring net-new users to monetizing their installed base. This week’s earnings suggest that this pressure is already here. Increasing ad density is one lever. Developing advertising that actually performs in a conversational experience is another. That will require more than slotting classic search ads into AI-generated answers. Consumers increasingly ask questions, refine their needs through follow-up prompts, and make decisions without navigating through lists of search results or navigating to vendors’ websites. Advertising must work differently in that environment. Google is responding by expanding ads in AI Mode and AI Overviews across more users and queries and experimenting with new ways to monetize AI-mediated search. Likewise, OpenAI is shifting ChatGPT from an incremental user growth story to a yield management story by adding ads that are visually separate from organic responses. After all, trust in ChatGPT’s answer is what makes OpenAI’s ad inventory valuable in the first place. Don’t Wait For Conversational Advertising To Mature Marketers shouldn’t treat conversational advertising as simply another media channel to test. As they continue to build out their advertising businesses, brands need to determine where conversational ads belong in their media plan, which budgets fund them, and how to measure advertising’s influence when AI mediates discovery and decision-making. Many of the Forrester clients we talk to are pulling from display budgets to test conversational advertising. In time, budgets for conversational ads may come from paid search and paid social. There are still plenty of unknowns. Which ad formats will consumers tolerate? How dense of an ad load can answer engines support? Will conversational advertising pull meaningful spend from paid search, further threatening Google’s cash cow, or will it generate a new source of funds? And what does an impression, click, or conversion even mean when an answer engine plays the biggest role in the path to purchase? Our 2027 research on conversational advertising will tackle these questions as this emerging channel takes shape. Request a guidance session to discuss your conversational advertising plans. Categories Advertising Age of the Customer AI Insights B2C Marketing

resources.headline: Six B2B Marketing Trends Shaping 2026
resources.fullText: Explore six B2B marketing trends shaping 2026 and discover where to invest to strengthen your pipeline, improve ROI, and accelerate growth. The B2B marketing trends for 2026 come down to six shifts. AI moves from experiment to budget line. Buyers form preferences long before they talk to sales. First-party data replaces borrowed audiences. Marketing and sales share one revenue scorecard. Human expertise, events and community carry the credibility that AI cannot fake. And paid search rewards advertisers who feed Google’s automation good signals. Below, each trend comes with the numbers behind it and what to do with it. Start with budgets, because they show what leaders actually believe. In the U.S., B2B digital ad spending is projected to grow 17.4% to $24.60 billion in 2026, according to eMarketer. The wider market is growing too: the IAB’s outlook study forecasts a 9.5% rise in total U.S. ad spend, with social media up 14.6%, connected TV up 13.8% and commerce media up 12.1%. Inside B2B teams, the priorities are clear. Content Marketing Institute research found that the top areas for increased investment are AI-powered marketing tools (45%), events and experiential marketing (33%) and owned media (32%). A 2026 benchmark survey covered by Demand Gen Report put AI tools at the top of the list, replacing account-based marketing from the year before. One more signal is easy to miss. The IAB found that 54% of marketers name customer acquisition as their top objective, down 10 points year over year, while the focus on driving repeat purchases rose to 25%. Growth is shifting from pure acquisition toward getting more from the customers already won. The pattern: money flows to AI and to human-led formats at the same time. That is not a contradiction. It is the core tension of 2026. Most B2B teams now use AI for three jobs: modeling which accounts fit, drafting content, and orchestrating channel automation. The gap between teams is not whether they use it. It is where they stop. The risk is real. A 2026 study from Ideas-Led Growth and Risk.net reported that 49% of marketers see a risk to brand reputation or voice when using generative AI. The same report describes a cultural split: senior decision-makers are bullish on scaling with AI, while the writers closest to the work worry about accuracy and voice. Both sides are right. Our practical rule is to let AI produce and let people decide: The larger story is architecture. DeepL’s CMO Steve Rotter argued in Marketing Week that agentic AI could become the new martech stack, filling gaps where systems are slow or rigid. If you are weighing that shift, a clear agentic AI strategy with governance up front keeps pilots from stalling. On the revenue side, the advantages of AI in sales show up fastest where marketing and sales share the same data. For a hands-on look at tooling, see our guide to the best B2B marketing AI tools and our breakdown of how human insight makes AI creative work better. By the time a buyer fills out a form, the shortlist is mostly set. That is why brand is no longer a separate conversation from performance. Two mechanisms stand out in this year’s research. Buyer enablement. Gartner’s Philip Black called buyer enablement a key trend for 2026 in Marketing Week, noting that B2B buyers penalize brands for poor digital experiences and prefer to find information themselves. Your website is now your best salesperson. It needs clear pricing logic, relevant proof, and answers for every member of the buying group. Visibility in AI answers. A Content Marketing Institute report points to research-backed thought leadership as the way to establish credibility before purchase intent exists. When buyers ask an AI assistant who to trust, the brands with original data and a consistent point of view get named. If you want the tactical side, our piece on AI SEO strategies for 2026 covers it. This is the logic behind what we call brand-backed performance: a sharp position makes every paid click, email and sales call cheaper to win. If your positioning is blurry, no channel fixes it. Our executive-level branding work starts exactly there. Privacy rules and browser changes have made rented audiences less reliable. eMarketer’s Marketing Data Trends 2026 lays out the direction for U.S. teams: build measurement on consented first-party data from your CRM, website, product, email and offline conversions, connect it through governed identity and server-side or privacy-preserving integrations, and treat platform attribution as directional rather than complete. Privacy is also an enterprise-wide concern, not a legal footnote. Cisco’s 2026 Data and Privacy Benchmark Study surveyed over 5,200 IT, technology and security professionals with privacy responsibilities across 12 markets, including the United States. Every trend above fails if marketing hands over leads that sales does not want. Alignment is moving from a slogan to a set of working agreements. The components are consistent across sources. Salesforce’s alignment guide recommends a shared ideal-customer profile and personas, a data-backed definition of a marketing-qualified lead, agreed sales follow-up timing, and required feedback on disqualified leads. Highspot’s guidance says to anchor both teams to the same outcomes: pipeline creation, conversion rates and deal progression. MarketingProfs’ interview with Jessica Buchwald adds the working mechanism. In her description of joint account reviews, sales brings behavioral signals, marketing brings ICP-based suppressions, and the shared scoring decides which accounts get attention. One meeting a month on these five numbers does more than another dashboard. As AI makes content cheap, credibility gets expensive. B2B buyers lean on people they trust. resources.fullText: Summary for this page A quick AI-generated overview extracted directly from the content of this page. View summary Account-Based Marketing (ABM) has proven itself as a high return strategy for B2B organizations aiming to drive targeted engagement, align sales and marketing teams, and secure high-value deals. While the theory of ABM is straightforward, implementing it successfully requires strategy, tools, and collaboration. Today, that also means starting from buying signals rather than static lists, so campaigns reach accounts while they are in-market. To help you visualize ABM in action, we’ll explore real-world examples of successful ABM campaigns and distill the best practices that led to their success. Each example is mapped to an ABM campaign type (1:1, 1:few or 1:many), with the result and the lesson to copy. ABM campaign examples at a glance Company ABM type Main tactic Result Key lesson SundaySky 1:few SalesIntel human-verified data and intent behind tailored campaigns to target accounts 220% increase in account ABM conversion rates Start with accurate data on the right decision-makers BetterCloud 1:many (data foundation) Replaced several data vendors with one source for account, contact, technology and intent data Saved over $100,000; replaced ZoomInfo and Demandbase One reliable data source cuts cost and improves targeting Snowflake 1:1 at scale 1:1 account pages, AdRoll ABM and LinkedIn ads, SDR e-gifts, 1:1 events 75% more SDR-booked meetings in ABM accounts (QoQ); 3x meeting rate in SDR-aligned 1:1 accounts Scale 1:1 by aligning SDRs with ABM Adobe 1:many (target-account paid social) Shared account focus on LinkedIn for marketing and Sales Navigator-led sales 42% of 2018 closed-won deals influenced by marketing on LinkedIn; LinkedIn-influenced deals 161% larger Marketing and sales work best from one account list Wilmington Paper 1:many Verified contacts and AI-assisted list building for campaign-ready audiences 68% increase in net-new pipeline; 7x ROI on influenced opportunities Fast, accurate audience building drives pipeline What is Account-Based Marketing? ABM flips traditional inbound marketing on its head by identifying specific, high-value accounts and tailoring personalized campaigns to engage them as “markets of one. Four elements make it work: account selection, personalization, multi-channel engagement, and account-level measurement. For the full framework, see our Account-Based Marketing guide. What is an ABM Campaign? An ABM (Account-Based Marketing) campaign is a highly targeted marketing initiative that concentrates organizational resources on a specific set of high-value accounts rather than a broad audience. By treating individual companies as “markets of one,” an ABM campaign utilizes personalized content and cross-team alignment between sales and marketing to engage key stakeholders within a target account. This precision-based strategy leverages buying signals, intent data and multi-channel outreach to accelerate the sales cycle and maximize return on investment (ROI) for complex B2B deals. ABM campaign types: 1:1, 1:few and 1:many ABM campaigns differ mainly in how many accounts each campaign serves. Each example below maps to one of three types. Type How it works Best for Example in this post 1:1 (strategic) A fully custom campaign for a single account, built with sales Must-win accounts with large deal potential Snowflake 1:few (cluster) One campaign for a small group of similar accounts, grouped by industry, use case or buying signal Tier-2 accounts that share a pain point SundaySky 1:many (programmatic) One campaign, personalized by data (industry, persona, signal), across a larger ICP list Broad ICP coverage without custom assets BetterCloud, Adobe, Wilmington Paper Most programs blend all three: 1:many campaigns reach the broad ICP, 1:few campaigns serve clusters, and 1:1 campaigns go to strategic accounts. Buying signals, such as an intent surge, a funding round or a leadership change, tell you when an account should move up a tier. Case Study 1: SundaySky’s 220% Conversion Leap with SalesIntel ABM type: 1:few · Timeframe: case study published October 2023 Objective: SundaySky, a leading video platform, aimed to enhance their ABM campaigns by effectively targeting high-value accounts to improve engagement and conversion rates. Approach: Data Accuracy Enhancement: SundaySky integrated SalesIntel’s human-verified data to ensure their outreach efforts were directed at the right decision-makers within target accounts. Personalized Campaigns: Leveraging precise data, SundaySky created highly tailored campaigns that resonated with their target audience, improving engagement. Strategic Data Integration: SalesIntel’s data solutions were embedded into SundaySky’s ABM workflows to streamline targeting and personalization. Results: A 220% increase in conversion rates from targeted campaigns. Enhanced audience engagement through personalized outreach. More efficient ABM processes powered by accurate data. Best Practice: Integrate human-verified data into ABM strategies to ensure targeted, personalized outreach to the right contacts. Today, pair that data with ICP lookalike modeling and buying signals, so the target list contains accounts that match your best customers and show in-market behavior. Many of them struggle to implement it effectively. This guide covers everything from initial setup to advanced B2B workflows.
